narrative: The model estimated a 15% chance that you will fail your final year. That is a low failing-risk estimate: it implies roughly an 85% chance of passing, so it does not by itself show that failing is likely or that remedial courses are automatically required. Among the factors that most influenced the estimate, the strongest was your record of past class failures: you have none, matching the average for students who passed. The next was your intention to pursue higher education: you want to continue, as did all passing students in the comparison. The third was weekend alcohol use: yours is very low, a pattern more common among passing students. All three therefore pushed the estimate toward passing rather than failing, so the model’s main drivers do not explain a fail prediction. The clearest area to watch is attendance: you have 9 absences versus an average of about 3.8 among passing students, so reducing absences would be sensible. Your weekly study time of 2–5 hours and family support are broadly typical. Given the low stated failing probability and protective top factors, ask the school what rule triggered mandatory remediation and whether attendance support or targeted help, rather than compulsory courses, is the better next step.
